strengths: The paper presents a useful extension of functional maps to tetrahedral volumes, connecting volumetric correspondence, boundary-driven connectivity transfer, and volume-aware surface matching. Compatibility with ZoomOut, CMH, and Orthoprods makes the framework potentially practical beyond a single application.

The strongest practical result is the reported recovery of 85% of 1,405 previously unsuccessful untangling cases by replacing the initialization (Section 5.2). This suggests substantial value as a component of an existing geometry-processing pipeline, even without guaranteed injectivity.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence of correspondence quality. On 40 volumetric pairs, Orthoprods achieves an average geodesic error of 0.0044, while Table 2 shows substantial surface-matching improvements on SHREC’19 and TOPKIDS across all three bases.

The manuscript includes useful implementation and diagnostic material: pseudocode, basis-size settings, runtime comparisons, per-pair flip curves, and additional continuity and coverage metrics. The discussion of tetrahedralization failures and excluded shapes is also valuable.
weaknesses: The central boundary-reconstruction justification is mathematically incorrect as stated. Section 4.1 and Appendix D claim that Neumann eigenfunctions have linearly independent boundary traces across the selected spectrum. On a ball, distinct radial Neumann eigenfunctions have constant, hence proportional, boundary traces. Having more boundary samples than basis functions does not establish independence either. Consequently, the asserted left inverse and recovery of interior coefficients from boundary values are not generally justified. The pseudoinverse remains a usable heuristic, but its rank, conditioning, and sensitivity require analysis; Appendix D’s surface reconstruction experiment does not establish these properties.

The injectivity claims exceed both the theory and the experiments. A complete spectral basis permits representation of arbitrary signals but does not make an estimated functional map bijective or determine an interior extension from its boundary. With the full discrete basis, the boundary restriction has fewer rows than columns whenever interior vertices exist. Thus, the claim in Section 6 that a sufficiently large spectrum can always achieve full injectivity is unsupported. Table 1 still reports 0.34–0.93% flipped cells at the largest tested size, and Figure 7 demonstrates selected successes rather than a general guarantee.

The claim of consistently superior surface matching is contradicted by Table 2. On SHREC’20, volumetric LBO increases AGE from 0.182 to 0.272, and Orthoprods increases it from 0.183 to 0.301; their pairwise success rates are only 14.84% and 8.24%. CMH improves this dataset, but these results support a conditional benefit dependent on the basis and tetrahedralization, rather than the abstract’s broad superiority claim. The discussion acknowledges some failures without reconciling the repeated general claim.

The connectivity-transfer evaluation does not sufficiently establish fidelity to the prescribed target boundary. Equations (7)–(9) perform truncated spectral reconstruction, which can move boundary vertices, yet the principal quantitative measure is the fraction of flipped tetrahedra. Boundary errors and distortion statistics are needed alongside untangling success to determine whether valid elements also represent the intended target domain. The 85% recovery experiment also lacks detailed reporting of boundary enforcement, stopping criteria, and total computational cost.

Some supporting evidence has narrower scope than the conclusions suggest. Volumetric correspondence is primarily evaluated on meshes sharing connectivity, leaving robustness to independent interior discretizations insufficiently quantified. Brain segmentation transfer is illustrated on two targets without anatomical accuracy measurements. Reproducibility is helped by the pseudocode, but descriptor construction, optimization settings, and geodesic-error normalization remain insufficiently specified. These limitations are secondary to the incorrect boundary-recovery argument and unsupported injectivity claims, which determine the weak-reject recommendation despite the promising empirical contribution.

strengths: Extending functional maps to tetrahedral volumes is a useful contribution to 3D correspondence. The framework supports signal transfer, connectivity transfer, and volume-aware surface matching while accommodating existing basis constructions and refinement algorithms.

The strongest practical result is the reported recovery of bijective maps in 85% of 1,405 previously failed untangling cases by replacing the initialization (Section 5.2). This suggests substantial value even without guaranteed injectivity.

The evaluation includes 40 volumetric shape pairs, several spectral bases, runtime measurements, and four surface-matching datasets. Table 2 shows meaningful improvements on SHREC’19 and TOPKIDS across all three bases; the supplementary material also reports coverage, continuity, and flipped elements.

The two connectivity-transfer constructions are clearly expressed through equations and pseudocode. Basis-size experiments and discussion of tetrahedralization failures help characterize practical tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The central boundary-recovery justification is incorrect as stated. Section 4.1 and Appendix D claim that Neumann eigenfunctions have linearly independent boundary traces across the selected spectrum. On a ball, distinct radial Neumann eigenfunctions have constant boundary traces, which are linearly dependent. Having more boundary samples than basis functions does not establish full column rank. Consequently, the claimed left inverse and recovery of interior coefficients require additional assumptions and conditioning analysis. Appendix D evaluates surface reconstruction, not this identifiability issue.

The injectivity claims exceed what the construction establishes. Sections 5.2 and 6 suggest that sufficiently many eigenfunctions can always yield an injective map. A complete spectral basis neither makes an arbitrary functional map correspond to a bijection nor uniquely determines interior coordinates from boundary data. In the discrete full-basis limit, the boundary restriction necessarily has fewer rows than columns when interior vertices exist. The empirical reduction of flips is valuable, but it does not support the stated guarantee.

The claim of consistently superior surface matching is contradicted by Table 2. On SHREC’20, volumetric LBO increases AGE from 0.182 to 0.272 and Orthoprods increases it from 0.183 to 0.301, winning only 14.84% and 8.24% of pairs, respectively. Two bases also underperform on VOL, although those errors are extremely small. The manuscript acknowledges some failures, but its abstract and conclusions still overstate the evidence. The supported result is a dataset- and basis-dependent advantage.

Validation of the principal volumetric contribution remains incomplete. The quantitative correspondence dataset uses identical connectivity, leaving robustness to independently discretized interiors insufficiently tested. Connectivity transfer is compared primarily through basis variants and a Tutte initialization; comparison with a standard harmonic or elastic interior extension would better isolate the benefit of the spectral construction. The important 85% untangling result also lacks a detailed breakdown of runtime, distortion, and solver settings.

The medical demonstration comprises two qualitative brain transfers without anatomical accuracy measurements or registration baselines. It establishes feasibility, but cannot substantiate reliable medical segmentation transfer. Likewise, Table 3 reports approximately 5.8–10.8% flipped tetrahedra for volumetric correspondence variants, limiting their direct use where valid deformation maps are required.

Overall, the useful empirical contribution is outweighed by the unsupported boundary-identifiability and injectivity arguments, together with incomplete validation of the claimed generality. These are material scientific concerns rather than presentation refinements and determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper develops a useful extension of functional maps to tetrahedral volumes, supporting volumetric correspondence, connectivity transfer, and volume-aware surface matching. Compatibility with ZoomOut, CMH, and Orthoprods makes the framework practically interesting.

The strongest practical result is the reported recovery of bijective maps for 85% of 1,405 previously failed untangling cases after spectral initialization (Section 5.2). This suggests meaningful utility beyond correspondence benchmarks.

Experiments demonstrate substantial surface-matching improvements on SHREC’19 and TOPKIDS across all three tested bases. For example, LBO average geodesic error decreases from 0.103 to 0.0664 on SHREC’19 and from 0.124 to 0.0885 on TOPKIDS.

The manuscript provides useful algorithmic pseudocode, basis-size experiments, runtime measurements, and supplementary map-quality metrics. Its discussion of tetrahedralization failures and computational costs helps establish practical limitations.
weaknesses: The central boundary-recovery justification is incorrect as stated. Section 4.1 and Appendix D assert that Neumann eigenfunctions have linearly independent boundary traces across the chosen spectrum. On a ball, distinct radial Neumann eigenfunctions all have constant boundary traces and are therefore dependent. Having more boundary samples than basis functions does not establish full column rank. Consequently, the claimed left inverse and stable recovery of interior coefficients do not follow; the pseudoinverse remains a heuristic whose conditioning and sensitivity are not evaluated.

The injectivity claims exceed what the method establishes. Sections 5.2 and 6 suggest that using sufficiently many eigenfunctions can always yield an injective map. A complete basis provides representational capacity, but does not make an estimated functional map bijective or resolve the ambiguity of interior extensions from boundary data. With the full discrete basis, boundary restriction is necessarily underdetermined when interior vertices exist. Table 1 supports decreasing average flip rates, not a general guarantee of eventual injectivity.

The claim of consistently superior surface matching contradicts Table 2. On SHREC’20, volumetric LBO worsens average error from 0.182 to 0.272, and Orthoprods from 0.183 to 0.301; they improve only 14.84% and 8.24% of pairs, respectively. CMH reverses this trend, making the benefit strongly basis-dependent. The accompanying discussion acknowledges these failures, but the abstract and overall conclusions still overgeneralize.

The connectivity-transfer evaluation does not isolate the advantage over simpler interior-extension methods, such as harmonic extension under the same boundary correspondences. The impressive untangling recovery result also lacks detailed end-to-end timing and solver settings. This matters because Table 1 reports 554–1,127 seconds for the largest bases, leaving the practical accuracy–cost advantage incompletely established.

Evidence for anatomical correspondence is limited to qualitative segmentation transfer on two brains, without overlap scores or registration comparisons. More broadly, the main volumetric correspondence benchmark uses shared connectivity, so robustness to independently generated interior meshes remains insufficiently characterized. Overall, the practical merits are worthwhile, but the incorrect recovery argument and unsupported injectivity claims concern core properties of the proposed method; together with the evaluation gaps, they favor weak rejection.
